title: Stability
notes: Open by framing stability as the reason persistence can be used as a measurement device rather than only a combinatorial invariant. The point is not that diagrams are unchanged, but that a controlled perturbation in the input produces a controlled perturbation in the output.

title: Learning Arc
notes: Use the arc as a contract for the lecture. First the algebra has to survive adjacent swaps in a filtration order; then the moving pairings become vineyards; then diagram metrics state stability; finally the same metric problem becomes an explicit bipartite matching algorithm.

title: Filtration Perturbation
notes: Read the diagram vertically. At each time t the ordered list of simplex values defines one filtration, while crossings mark the only instants where the order changes. The infinity norm band is the measurement of how far two endpoint functions can pull any simplex.

title: Boundary Matrix Ledger
notes: This slide keeps the algebra honest before any stability theorem appears. A filtration order gives a boundary matrix, reduction records unique low entries, and the check boundary squared zero makes the persistence pairs legitimate algebraic evidence rather than a drawing convention.

title: Transpositions And Switches
notes: Emphasize that a generic one-parameter family changes the order only by adjacent transpositions. Most swaps merely rename neighboring columns, but the critical cases force a column addition and switch two persistence pairings. That local repair is the engine behind vineyards.

title: Vineyards
notes: A vineyard is the movie of persistence diagrams along a one-parameter family. Each vine tracks a birth-death pair until it reaches the endpoint diagram or the diagonal. Students should notice that continuity of the function values turns pair changes into continuous paths.

title: Bottleneck Distance
notes: Define bottleneck distance as the best possible worst matched displacement, allowing unmatched off-diagonal features to pair with the diagonal. The square picture is useful because a candidate epsilon succeeds exactly when every selected point can be assigned inside its infinity-norm square.

title: Stability Theorem For Filtrations
notes: State the theorem as a measurement guarantee. The proof idea is visible from the vineyard: each simplex value moves with slope bounded by the endpoint infinity norm, so every vine endpoint moves by at most that bound in birth and death coordinates.

title: Tame Functions
notes: Move from finite filtrations to functions by looking at sublevel sets. Tameness says there are only finitely many homological event levels and finite ranks, so the diagram remains a finite off-diagonal ledger plus the diagonal reservoir needed for matching.

title: Wasserstein Distance
notes: Contrast Wasserstein with bottleneck carefully. Bottleneck ignores how many small wrinkles appear if the largest displacement stays small, while Wasserstein sums all those costs. This is why extra hypotheses are needed before a Wasserstein stability statement can be trusted.

title: Lipschitz / Total Persistence
notes: The Lipschitz theorem uses geometry of the domain to prevent infinitely many meaningful wrinkles from accumulating. Polynomial growth of triangulations gives bounded total persistence, and that bound converts the bottleneck control into a Wasserstein estimate with an exponent depending on q and k.

title: Curves As Height Functions
notes: For the curve application, fix one direction and turn a closed curve into a height function on the circle. The zero-dimensional diagram counts sublevel components, and total persistence measures how long those components remain alive as horizontal lines sweep across the curve.

title: Cauchy-Crofton And Curvature
notes: This slide translates geometry into countable events. Cauchy-Crofton recovers length by averaging line intersections, while total curvature is recovered by averaging critical points of height functions. Persistence enters because those same intersections and critical points are encoded by height diagrams.

title: Persistence Proof Of Generalized Fary
notes: Walk through the proof pipeline rather than expanding every integral. Frechet closeness gives uniform closeness of every directional height function, stability bounds matched persistence changes, and integrating those changes converts the bound into the generalized Fary inequality.

title: Diagram Distance As Matching
notes: Now make the metric computational. Off-diagonal points from one diagram, off-diagonal points from the other, and their diagonal copies form a balanced bipartite graph. Bottleneck asks for the smallest threshold with a perfect matching; Wasserstein asks for minimum total cost.

title: Augmenting Paths And Cost Matching
notes: Close by connecting the algebraic metric to algorithms students can inspect. Augmenting paths increase a matching one step at a time, binary search finds the bottleneck threshold, and the cost version adjusts potentials so zero modified-cost augmentations eventually yield a minimum-cost perfect matching.
